newsitem.title: USA: IPO VIEW - Despite Hertz success, market selective.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - Despite Hertz success, market selective.

text.p: Enthusiasm for new issues is likely to be tempered this week despite Hertz Corp.'s roaring market debut Friday.

Among the companies at bat for initial public offerings this week are golf sportswear maker Pivot Rules Inc., specialty financing firm Long Beach Financial Corp., and Piranha Interactive Publishing Inc., a publisher of educational and entertainment software.

Hertz, the world's largest car rental company and a unit of Ford Motor Co., raised more than $400 million Friday and its new shareholders reaped a neat profit of more than 15 percent on its first day of trading.
The stock jumped by $3.75 to $27.75 from the offering price of $24, which priced at the top of expectations of $21 to $24.

"In times of uncertainty, as we are in now in the new-issues market, it is welcome to have an ... internationally known name of high quality like Hertz," said David Menlow, president of the IPO Financial Network.
Some analysts had said the IPO should have been priced even higher by underwriter J.P. Morgan & Co Inc..
But Menlow said before the pricing: "If (Hertz) prices at $24, that's not a sign of weakness. It's a sign that J.P. Morgan is looking to price the deal fairly in a market that is very tenuous."
Demand was high enough that J.P. Morgan exercised its "green shoe" option to buy an additional 2.61 million shares.

The issue of pricing is a sticky one for underwriters, who want to raise as much money as possible for their client company but also want to reward IPO buyers with high returns. Generally, only a firm's best clients get access to IPOs.
Lately, premiums have been weak. So if a deal is priced too high, an underwriter risks upsetting its best clients with a razor-thin premium or worse, a loss when the stock opens for trading.
When the IPO market was more speculative last year, higher prices tended to generate even higher demand, creating buying frenzies when IPOs opened.

But the current overall market will not catch fire from Hertz. It remains highly selective, favoring only strong companies with established financials and large-size deals that offer substantial liquidity, analysts said.
Few of the generally small-size issues on deck this week should stir demand as the market remains lackluster.
"It's the same old ... script of what we have been seeing lately. It should be pretty dull except for rare high quality issues," said John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket newsletter.
About 20 companies are on deck to go public this week, but most are likely to see their launch dates pushed further into the future.
Last week, four IPOs went public, raising $519 million, according to MCM CorporateWatch.

Fitzgibbon said he expects Weider Nutrition International Inc., an IPO underwritted by Credit Suisse First Boston, the most likely to stir interest with a forecast premium of 1/2 point. The company, based in Salt Lake City, Utah, makes nutritional supplements.
"There's a lot of issues being carried 'TBA,' or to be announced. That means, if the window opens, they will slam those deals through," said Fitzgibbon.
Currently, about 40 offerings are said to be "TBA" by underwriting desks.
